title: Integration: How We Know What We Know
objective: After this level you can connect each major astronomical discovery to the tool or method behind it.
summary: We can’t visit the stars, so astronomers read their light: spectra, parallax, transits, spin and gravitational waves.

cards.headline: We can’t visit the stars. So how do we know so much about them?
cards.body: We can visit only a few nearby worlds. Almost everything else we know, we read from the light and other signals that reach us.

items.label: What stars are made of
points: Spectral lines in their light: each element leaves its own set

items.label: Distance to nearby stars
points: Parallax: a star’s slight shift as Earth orbits the Sun

items.label: Planets around other stars
points: Transits (a dip in starlight) and wobbles (a star tugged back and forth)

cards.headline: New windows
cards.body: Some discoveries needed brand-new kinds of clues. Stars at galaxies’ edges orbit too fast for the visible matter to hold them, which gave away dark matter, something no one has ever seen. Redshift in galaxies’ light revealed the expanding universe. And in 2015 LIGO first detected gravitational waves from merging black holes: not light at all, but ripples in spacetime. Astronomy learned to feel the universe shake.

cards.headline: Old tricks still work
cards.body: And some clues needed no telescope at all. Around 240 BCE, Eratosthenes estimated Earth’s size by comparing the Sun’s noon angle in two Egyptian cities. A shadow, some geometry, and he had measured a planet without leaving it. From a shadow in Alexandria to a ripple in spacetime, it’s the same game: measure carefully, then reason carefully.

cards.headline: Methods: mastered
learned: Spectral lines reveal what stars are made of
Parallax measures distances to nearby stars

questions.prompt: Which pairing of method and discovery is correct?

options.label: Spectral lines → what stars are made of
Parallax → what stars are made of
Redshift → what planets are made of

questions.explanation: Each element leaves its own lines in a spectrum, so spectra reveal what stars are made of.

questions.prompt: An astronomer wants the distance to a nearby star. Which method fits best?

options.label: Listening for gravitational waves
options.rationale: Those come from colliding black holes and neutron stars.

questions.explanation: Parallax, the star’s tiny shift as Earth orbits the Sun, gives the distance to nearby stars.

questions.prompt: From Level 85: no one has ever seen dark matter. What evidence convinced astronomers it exists?

options.label: Photos of dark clouds between galaxies
options.rationale: Dark matter is invisible, not dark-colored.

options.label: Radio signals from dark matter itself
Stars orbiting faster than visible mass allows

questions.explanation: Galaxies spin too fast for their visible matter, so extra unseen mass must be adding gravity.
